source: When only gravity and springs do work, K + U stays the same.
Students think a heavier object reaches the bottom of a frictionless ramp with a higher speed.

The work-energy theorem counts the work of every force. Gravity's work and a spring's work can be tracked instead as changes in gravitational and elastic potential energy. If nothing else does work, the total stays fixed.

When only gravity and springs do work, the mechanical energy is conserved: $\role[starting kinetic energy]{energy}{K_i} + \role[starting potential energy]{energy}{U_i} = \role[final kinetic energy]{energy}{K_f} + \role[final potential energy]{energy}{U_f}$, with $U = U_g + U_s$.

Gravity's work on the object is $-\Delta U_g$ and the spring's is $-\Delta U_s$. If they are the only forces doing work, the work-energy theorem gives $-\Delta U_g - \Delta U_s = \Delta K$, so $\Delta K + \Delta U = 0$. Normal forces on a frictionless track and the tension in a pendulum string are perpendicular to the motion, so they do no work and don't spoil this.
A cart on a frictionless track: K and Ug trade back and forth, and their total stays fixed.
A child starts from rest at the top of a frictionless slide $5\ \text{m}$ high. Find the speed at the bottom.
A coaster moves at $4\ \text{m/s}$ on a $30\ \text{m}$ hill. Ignoring friction, how fast is it on the next hill, $18\ \text{m}$ high?
A spring with $k = 800\ \text{N/m}$ compressed $10\ \text{cm}$ launches a $0.2\ \text{kg}$ ball horizontally. Find its launch speed.

Thinking a heavier object reaches the bottom of a frictionless ramp with a higher speed. It has more energy, but it needs more energy for each m/s: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2$, and the mass cancels. Check: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ has no $m$ in it.
